items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: The colour for sodium is described as yellow in the specification, but you will also see it described as orange. Both are usually acceptable.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: Lithium isn't the only ion to give a red flame colour. Strontium gives a very similar colour. The only way to be sure is to compare the flame colour next to the flame colour of a known compound of lithium or strontium.

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection and take great care with the concentrated acid. Do not get it on your skin and watch out for 'spitting' when heating it on the wire.

items.label: section_header
items.text: TESTING FOR CATIONS (POSITIVE IONS) USING SODIUM HYDROXIDE SOLUTION

items.label: text
items.text: Of the common hydroxides, only sodium, potassium and ammonium hydroxides dissolve in water to any extent. Most metal hydroxides are insoluble. That means that if you add sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing the metal ions, you will get a precipitate of the metal hydroxide.

items.label: text
items.text: To carry out this test, you dissolve the salt in distilled (pure) water and put about 1 cm³ in a test-tube. Add about the same volume of dilute sodium hydroxide solution. What you are looking for in most of these tests is the formation of a precipitate; the solution will go cloudy as a solid forms.

items.label: text
items.text: Formation of a blue precipitate shows the presence of copper(Il) ions. The precipitate is copper(Ill) hydroxide.

items.label: formula
items.text: C u ^ { 2 + ( a q ) } + 2 O H \text {-} ( a q ) \to C u ( O H ) _ { 2 } ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: Any copper(ll) salt in solution will react with sodium hydroxide solution in this way. For example, with copper(ll) sulfate solution, the full equation is:

items.label: text
items.text: CuSO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na2SO4(aq)

items.label: text
items.text: Formation of an orange-brown precipitate shows the presence of iron(Ill) ions (Fe³+). The precipitate is iron(III) hydroxide.

items.label: text
items.text: Fe³+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)

items.label: text
items.text: Any iron(Ill) compound in solution will give this precipitate. An example of a full equation might be:

items.label: text
items.text: FeCl3(aq) + 3NaOH(aq)→ Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq)

items.label: text
items.text: Notice how much more complicated the full equations for these reactions are. They also hide what is going on. Use ionic equations for precipitation reactions wherever possible.
